newsitem.title: BULGARIA: FEATURE - Bulgarian lev gains from peg to weak mark.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Bulgarian lev gains from peg to weak mark.

text.p: The first month of operation of Bulgaria's currency board regime has brought stability and signs of a revival in the banking sector, as well as some benefits from a weakening anchor currency, the mark.

The fixed exchange rate mechanism is part of reforms agreed with the International Monetary Fund after a run on the lev amid political and economic chaos last winter. It requires levs in circulation to be backed by central bank foreign exchange reserves, pegging it at 1,000 to the mark.

"We are extremely happy with the introduction of the currency board," said World Bank resident representative Alberto Musalem. "No one could have anticipated that the inflation rate would come down so quickly. There has been a very positive response from investors."
Financier Emil Harsev said the weak mark had helped give the lev a "soft landing" in the currency board introduced on July 1, permitting more levs to go into circulation.

"The current fall in the mark is exceptionally beneficial for Bulgaria because it prevented a sudden halt in inflation at a time when the currency board was being introduced and allowed Bulgaria to take a more flexible approach towards implementation of the system," he said.
GOOD FOR EXPORTS, BAD FOR IMPORTS

Krassen Stanchev, executive director of the Institute for Market Economics, said exports benefited, particularly to countries where trade was not denominated in marks, such as the former Soviet Union and the Middle East.

On the minus side, raw materials and energy denominated in dollars make up some 35 percent of Bulgarian imports, and domestic debt becomes more expensive because of the component held in dollar-denominated domestic government securities.
"The positive and negative aspects neutralise one another," Stanchev said.
The lev has been trading in a range of 994-996 per mark since the start of the currency board, as foreign currency supply from banks and clients outweighs demand.

Foreign currency demand from clients like fuel and energy importers is traditionally low in summer and the central bank has been seen as the main foreign currency buyer at the 995 levs per mark fixed bid under the currency board.
The lev is expected to trade near the 1,000 levs per mark asking rate of the central bank in autumn and winter when fuel and energy importers seek large foreign currency volumes.
Lev rates against other foreign currencies are calculated according to the domestic lev/mark rate and the mark crosses against the currencies on global markets.
Some dealers expect the lev peg may eventually be adjusted.

"As the rate of 1,000 levs per mark seems to be too strong for the lev I expect a change of the fixed rate to around 1,200 levs per mark some time in the future, adjusting to the inflation that will be accumulated after the introduction of the board," one dealer said.
SIGNS OF CONSUMER LOAN REVIVAL

At the same time, Bulgaria is taking steps to stabilise its banking system after a wave of insolvencies last year. The currency board makes tighter financial discipline inevitable as it bans lending from the central bank to commercial banks except in cases of systemic risk.
Stanchev said there were signs that cash-rich banks would start providing consumer credits for the first time since 1991.
The State Savings Bank announced last week that it would offer loans at an annual interest rate of 9.5 percent, compared to the central bank annual main interest rate of 5.42 percent.

The economy had already stabilised in anticipation of the currency board's introduction from July 1. Monthly inflation declined to 0.8 percent in June from highs of 243 percent in February when the lev went into freefall.

Margarita Michailova, manager of a central Sofia grocery, said importers of dollar-denominated goods had raised their prices by some 15-20 percent since July 1, and Bulgarian producers were increasing their prices to cover losses accumulated in the first five months of the year.

"A lot of people expected price cuts and high wages immediately after the currency board was introduced, but the currency board is not a magic wand and we still live in the same country which is still in deep economic crisis," said Sofia HiFi equipment seller Vladimir Todorov.
